blocks.prompt: The Bus That Had to Be Yellow
blocks.text: The school bus is yellow for a reason. Long ago, buses were red, or blue, or white, or green. Every town picked its own color. Then a teacher named Frank Cyr had an idea. He asked people to pick one color for every bus in the country. They hung strips of paint on a wall and looked at them for a long time. They chose bright yellow. Yellow is the color your eyes find first, even when the sky is still gray and sleepy. Black words look sharp on yellow too. So now the bus is yellow in every town, and everyone knows what it is.

blocks.prompt: The Bus That Can Stop Traffic
blocks.text: A school bus does something no other vehicle on the road can do. It can stop traffic. Watch the lights. When the bus is getting ready to stop, yellow lights flash on the front and the back. That is a warning to the cars behind it. Then the bus stops, red lights flash, and a stop sign swings out from its side on a metal arm. Now the law says every car must wait, in both directions, until the arm folds back in. Why go to all that trouble? Because the most dangerous place near a school bus is not inside it. It is the ten feet of road all around it, where a driver in a car might not see a small person. So the bus makes itself impossible to miss. It flashes, it swings out an arm, and it wears the brightest color anyone could find. Inside, the bus is quieter about its job. The seats are tall and padded and packed close together, like a row of soft walls. If the bus ever stopped hard, those seats would catch you.

blocks.prompt: Seven Days and Forty Four Rules
blocks.text: In 1939, a school bus could be almost any color. It might be a truck with a wooden body bolted on by the local carpenter. It might be painted red because red paint was cheap that year. Nothing matched, nothing was tested, and nobody had written down what a bus for children should actually be. Frank Cyr noticed. He was a professor who had traveled thousands of miles through rural America looking at how children got to school, and what he saw worried him. So he did something practical. He got a grant, invited the people who mattered, and put them all in one room. For seven days in April 1939, engineers, paint makers, and officials from every state argued about buses at Teachers College in New York. They hung strips of paint along the walls, dozens of shades of yellow and orange, and studied them. They settled on one: a bright yellow that would later be called National School Bus Glossy Yellow. It was not chosen because it was pretty. Human eyes pick up yellow out of the corner of your eye faster than almost any other color, which matters at seven in the morning when the light is thin and gray. Black lettering also reads cleanly against it, so the words SCHOOL BUS could be seen from far away. That week produced forty four standards in total, covering everything from ceiling height to the width of the aisle. Almost every yellow bus on the road today is still following rules written by people in a room with paint strips on the walls.

notes: Compartmentalization: the seats do the job a belt would do
Tall padded seats set deliberately close together
Heavy and high, so most car impacts land below the riders
Most injuries happen outside the bus, not inside it
The crossing gate pushes kids forward into the driver's view

blocks.prompt: Why the Seats Are So Close Together
blocks.text: Ride in a car and you buckle a belt across your body. Ride in a school bus and, in most of the country, you do not. Parents notice this and it bothers them, which is fair. The reason is not laziness or cost, though cost is part of the argument. The reason is a design idea called compartmentalization. Look at the seats on a school bus. They are unusually tall, thickly padded, and set close together, closer than seems comfortable. That spacing is deliberate. Each row of seats builds a padded box around the child behind it. In a sudden stop, a passenger moves forward a short distance and meets a seat back engineered to absorb the energy of the impact rather than resist it. No buckle required, and no chance of a child fastening the belt wrong or unbuckling it three miles from home. The bus helps itself in other ways. It is heavy, so it loses less speed in a collision with a smaller vehicle. It sits high, so the passengers are above the level where most car impacts land. It is stiff and boxy, and the frame is built to hold up if it rolls. The numbers back the design. Federal safety researchers report that a student is far more likely to reach school safely on a bus than in the family car. School buses are, by the ordinary measures, the safest vehicles on the American road. There is a catch, and it is the part that matters most. Most children hurt in school bus incidents are not hurt while riding. They are hurt in the ten feet of pavement surrounding the bus, struck by passing cars or by the bus itself, in the moments when they are walking to a door or crossing in front of a bumper. Everything loud about a school bus, the yellow paint, the red flashers, the arm with the stop sign on it, the gate that swings out from the front bumper to push children forward where the driver can see them, exists for those few seconds. The bus is safe. The road around the bus is not, and no seat belt can help with that.

meta.templateLabel: The Bus That Had to Be Yellow

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Before engines there was the kid hack, a horse drawn school wagon
Rear door so the driver never let go of the reins
National School Bus Glossy Yellow, set April 1939
Roughly half a million buses run in the US
Buses stop at every railroad crossing, doors open
Electric buses cost more to buy, far less to run

blocks.prompt: From the Kid Hack to the Electric Bus
blocks.text: Before the yellow bus, there was the kid hack. In the 1880s, American farm children reached school in a horse drawn wagon with benches down each side and a door at the back, cut there so the driver never had to leave the reins to let anyone in. The name came from hackney, an old word for a carriage for hire. The kid hack was slow, cold, and open to the weather, and it was still an improvement on walking four miles through snow. When engines replaced horses, the wagon body simply moved onto a truck frame. The result was not a school bus so much as a truck with something built on it, usually by a local shop, out of wood, to no standard at all. Buses were red, green, white, or whatever paint the shop had. Some had doors that opened into traffic. Some had none. Nobody had ever written down what a vehicle carrying other people's children ought to be, because until then nobody thought it was their job. Frank Cyr thought it was. A professor at Teachers College in New York, Cyr had spent years surveying how rural children got to school, and he had seen enough. In 1939 he took a grant from the Rockefeller Foundation, gathered engineers, state transportation officials, and paint company chemists, and put them in a room together for a week. The famous decision was the color. The group hung painted strips along the wall, dozens of yellows and oranges, and picked the shade now known as National School Bus Glossy Yellow. The logic was cold and practical: the human eye detects yellow in peripheral vision, the blurry edge of what we see, more readily than red, and black lettering stays legible against it. A bus is most often loading in the half light of early morning, exactly when a driver's peripheral vision is doing most of the work. The color was not a mood. It was a calculation. The color gets remembered because it is visible. The other forty three standards agreed that week mattered more: aisle widths, ceiling heights, seat dimensions, the shape of the body. They turned a local craft product into a national machine with a specification. The specification kept growing. Modern buses are built around compartmentalization, in which tall padded seats spaced closely together form energy absorbing compartments, so the vehicle protects passengers through its own structure rather than through belts. Roof strength, joint strength, and fuel system integrity are all tested. Buses stop at every railroad crossing, doors open, engine quiet, driver listening. The crossing gate on the front bumper swings out to force a child far enough forward to be seen. Each rule exists because somewhere, once, its absence cost something. The next change is already arriving, and it is under the floor. Roughly half a million school buses run in the United States, most of them burning diesel, and children breathe that exhaust twice a day at the age when their lungs are still developing. Electric buses have no tailpipe at all. They cost far more to buy and far less to run, and a fleet that drives the same route every day and sits parked all night happens to be almost the ideal machine to electrify. Federal money is now pushing thousands of them onto the road. The bus will stay yellow. That part was settled in a room in 1939 by people looking at paint strips on a wall, and it turned out they were right.
